#2038. Alverca vs Casa Pia - prediction, team news, lineups

By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 05 Nov 2026 23:29

Alverca will be looking to avoid a fourth consecutive defeat in all competitions when they welcome Casa Pia to the Complexo Desportivo FC Alverca on Saturday evening for their Liga Portugal Matchday 11 encounter.

Sergio Ferreira's side sit 10th in the Primeira Liga table, four points and six places above their visitors, who currently occupy one of the two outright relegation spots.

Alverca's second consecutive campaign in the Portuguese top flight has been characterised by spells of inconsistency, with a three-match winning run against Nacional, Rio Ave and Famalicao between mid-September and October sandwiched between winless periods.

Ferreira's men had failed to win any of their opening five fixtures before finding their feet, but they have since returned to familiar struggles after losing their last three outings without scoring, beginning with a Taca de Portugal elimination at the hands of lower-league Tondela before suffering successive 1-0 league losses to Arouca and Benfica.

Looking to avoid a third consecutive defeat in the top-flight for the first time since December 2025, the Ribatejo outfit must also find greater balance at both ends of the pitch, having scored 13 goals and conceded 14 in 10 Primeira Liga matches, with multiple strikes coming just once and only one clean sheet recorded during that period.

Alverca’s home form has offered little encouragement either, as Ferreira's side have managed just one victory in five matches on their own turf this season (D2, L2), with their most recent outing at the venue ending in defeat to Arouca.

The hosts can nevertheless draw some confidence from previous results in this fixture, having won both league meetings with the Geese last season, recording a 2-0 victory in Rio Maior before following it up with a 3-1 success on home soil in April.

Casa Pia find themselves in a similarly difficult position after finishing 16th last season and securing their top-flight status through the relegation playoff, with their disappointing start to the current campaign largely down to shortcomings at both ends of the pitch.

Filipe Coelho's men have scored a joint-league-low five goals in the Primeira Liga this term, while only Maritimo (20) and Rio Ave (23) have conceded more than Os Gansos' 19, with their lack of cutting edge in attack once again evident in last weekend's 2-0 defeat to Sporting Lisbon.

There are, however, signs of improvement compared to their opening six fixtures, during which the Geese went without a victory, having now won two of their last four league matches and three of their most recent five across all competitions, including a Taca de Portugal triumph over lower-league Alpendorada.

A return to the road this weekend could also work in the visitors' favour, considering all seven of their league points this season have come away from home, with those results arriving across their last three trips, including a 2-0 victory over Estrela Amadora on their most recent outing.

Alverca remain without Bastien Meupiyou and Sabit Abdulai, who are both sidelined through injury, while goalkeeper Jhonatan Luiz and midfielder Rayan Lucas are doubts after completing modified training sessions earlier this week.

Steven Baseya and Andre Vidigal are available again after serving their respective suspensions, providing Ferreira with two additional options as he considers his selection for Saturday's encounter.

For Casa Pia, goalkeeper Andre Gomes appears to be the only confirmed absentee, while Jeremy Livolant is pushing for a starting place after playing 45 minutes against Sporting.

David Sousa is also one booking away from suspension, having collected four yellow cards this season, and another caution on Saturday would rule him out of the Taca de Portugal fourth-round meeting with Atletico CP on November 21.

Henrique Araujo could retain his place as the central striker, although Coelho also has Alasanna Jatta and veteran forward Cassiano available as alternative options.

Sequeira; Geraldes, Kaly, Sousa, Rosas; Perez, Ofori; Boukammiri, Rego, Pauwels; Araujo

Alverca have struggled to find the net in recent weeks, while their home record offers little reason to expect a convincing response, particularly against opponents who have collected all their league points on their travels this season.

Casa Pia have also lacked consistency in front of goal, but their recent away performances suggest that they are capable of making life difficult for the hosts, and a closely fought draw could be on the cards.

#2036. Official: Baresi honoured by City of Milano with inscription in the Famedio

Franco Baresi’s passing has left a hole in the hearts of AC Milan fans, but also of those in the city of Milano.

Some footballers transcend the game, especially those who become something else. For Baresi, football allowed him to offer more to the city that raised him through his extensive charity work. However, it wasn’t just the citizens of Milano who benefited from this.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Through the Fondazione Milan, the former defender helped people across the globe and that is why he’s considered so highly.

He was an excellent defender, perhaps an even better servant to the Rossoneri, but he was above all, he was a fantastic man. It speaks volumes that tributes still arrive for him and that the city stood still on the day of his service.

Baresi has already been remembered with murals, but the City of Milan have now offered their own memorial to one of its greatest sons, as the club detailed in a statement this afternoon.

“The City of Milano today honoured Franco Baresi, AC Milan’s legendary Captain, by inscribing his name in the Famedio at the Monumental Cemetery, a memorial dedicated to the figures who have shaped the city’s history and identity.

“The ceremony, led by Mayor Giuseppe Sala and City Council President Elena Buscemi, took place in the presence of Franco Baresi’s family and AC Milan Legend and Brand Ambassador Daniele Massaro, representing the Club.

“Baresi was honoured alongside 13 other distinguished figures, recognising both his extraordinary achievements on the pitch and the values he represented to generations of supporters and the wider Milan community.

“Born in Travagliato, near Brescia, Franco Baresi devoted his life to AC Milan and the city of Milano from a young age. He played a defining role in one of the greatest eras in football history. The Club retired his number 6 shirt in his honour and celebrated his 50 years with AC Milan in 2024. He had served as Honorary Vice President since 2020.

“Others honoured this year include Ornella Vanoni, a devoted Rossoneri supporter, Bruno Pizzul, Giovanni Gastel and Don Antonio Mazzi, alongside prominent figures from Milano’s cultural and civic life.

“Since December 2024, as part of the Club’s 125th anniversary celebrations, the Famedio’s Crypt has also been the final resting place of AC Milan founder Herbert Kilpin, alongside other figures who have shaped the city’s history, including Giuseppe Meazza, Giorgio Gaber, Enzo Jannacci and Alda Merini.

“The tribute to Franco Baresi goes far beyond football. It reflects the deep bond between AC Milan and Milano, a city whose history, social fabric and cultural identity the Club has helped shape for more than 125 years.”

#2035. RB Leipzig vs Augsburg - prediction, team news, lineups

By Anthony Nolan | 05 Nov 2026 23:32, Last updated: 06 Nov 2026 05:12

Desperate to end their Bundesliga slump, Augsburg will travel to face RB Leipzig at Red Bull Arena on Saturday.

Die Roten Bullen are hoping to bounce back from their midweek defeat, with Die Fuggerstadter winless in six league games.

Martin Demichelis's Leipzig currently sit fourth in the German top flight with 15 points to their name, just three shy of Borussia Dortmund and leaders Bayern Munich.

The Saxons have also been flawless in the league at Red Bull Arena, where they are yet to concede in domestic competition, not to mention that only Bayern have bettered their 22-goal tally in the Bundesliga so far.

However, Demichelis is facing intense criticism from the media in Leipzig, who have directly questioned the manager's position, prompting him to state that if he does not achieve the club's aims then he will leave of his own accord at the end of the season.

Former Roten Bullen boss Marco Rose - now of Bournemouth - also spoke out about the level of pressure on Demichelis, noting that, "If you know the media landscape a bit, you already get the feeling that the thumbs are down."

The Cherries' head coach then went on to reveal how the end of his tenure at Red Bull Arena "Did something" to him, and caused him to lose a bit of his "Lightness."

Last time out, Leipzig were beaten 3-2 by Manchester City in a Champions League thriller, bringing a three-game winning streak to an end, and marking the first time the hosts conceded on home turf this season.

Victory this weekend would be a fourth in five matches for Demichelis, and may even put Die Roten Bullen level with Dortmund and Bayern, though another defeat is likely to trigger a new wave of criticism.

Meanwhile, Manuel Baum's Augsburg kicked off their season in strong fashion with back-to-back triumphs, but have since endured a dire winless run in the Bundesliga.

Die Fuggerstatder last took all three points by thrashing Eintracht Frankfurt 4-1 on September 6, losing three and drawing three of their league games since.

The only bright spot during that stretch was a 4-2 DFB-Pokal success against Grossaspach, though it was followed up by a 2-1 defeat to Freiburg at WWK Arena just four days later.

Heading into Saturday's showdown, Augsburg are 10th in the Bundesliga with nine points, putting them just one shy of the top half but level with every club down to 15th-placed Hamburger SV, and only two points above Union Berlin in the relegation playoff spot.

This weekend's visitors will arrive as the underdogs, but the more optimistic amongst the travelling support could take heart from the fact Baum's side have earned three of their four wins across all competitions away from home.

Leipzig will be without striker Marc Guiu once again as he recovers from a hamstring injury, while winger Antonio Nusa is a doubt after being substituted against Man City as a precautionary measure, with manager Demichelis saying that the 21-year-old "Was close to getting injured."

Nusa could start on the left of the Saxons' attack this weekend, but if he is not ready to feature, then Tidiam Gomis could take his place in the XI.

Elsewhere, left-back Max Finkgrafe is a doubt with a thigh issue, and midfielder Assan Ouedraogo remains sidelined due to a shoulder injury.

In their absence, David Raum should start on the left of the Saxons' defence, while Neil El Aynaoui and Rocco Reitz operate in Leipzig's double pivot.

As for Augsburg, they are light at the back given that centre-halves Noahkai Banks (knee), Calvin Brackelmann (concussion) and Abdulai Juma Bah (suspension) are all unavailable.

Filling the gaps, Baum could opt for Jeffrey Gouweleeuw, Yannik Keitel and Chrislain Matsima to form his defence, with Robin Fellhauer and Hennes Behrens as wing-backs.

Vandevoordt; Henrichs, Orban, Lukeba, Raum; El Aynaoui, Reitz; Gomis, Nkunku, Nusa; Romulo

Dahmen; Gouweleeuw, Keitel, Matsima; Fellhauer, Massengo, Rieder, Behrens; Kade, Ibrahimovic; Gregoritsch

Leipzig may have been beaten by Man City in midweek, but their record at Red Bull Arena speaks for itself, and they should be able to get the better of their struggling opponents on Saturday.

Augsburg will be desperate for a win this weekend, yet they arrive as significant underdogs against a team that have not conceded on home turf in the league.

#2034. John Clark's granddaughter opens up on bid to immortalise Lisbon Lion with statue

"People knew the Lisbon Lion, but to me he was just grandad"’ says Clare Clark, articulating how it felt to be the apple of the eye of a Celtic legend.

“I still tear up every time I think or talk about him. It has been really hard since he left us last year. He was just such a big part of my life.”

John Clark passed away at the age of 84 in June last year. A surgeon in urology, his granddaughter still finds it hard to process the loss.

As a medical student at Aberdeen University, she would maintain the long-established practice of calling the old Bhoy every night at 10pm. Just to check in and get a rundown on his day.

“I actually called him Gan Gan. He was always just Gan Gan to me. So much so that when my mum or my gran talk about him even now they still refer to him as GG. It stuck.

“He was one of the driest and funniest men you could meet. He would always have a sly wee one liner that he delivered so softly it was easy to miss it altogether.”

The best story told about Clark – Luggy to friends and team-mates – dates back to the summer of 1981. Celtic were in New York to compete in the Trans-Atlantic Challenge Cup, a four team pre-season tournament also featuring the New York Cosmos, Seattle Sounders and Southampton.

In a hotel lift, winger Davie Provan was standing with the club’s assistant manager of the time when the doors opened and Pele, arguably the greatest footballer of all time, walked in.

Performing promotion duties for Escape To Victory, the Brazilian icon recognised a former opponent from a friendly international between Scotland and Brazil at Hampden prior to the 1966 World Cup.

“Scotland, Hampden, you number six – a very good player,” said Pele in warm tones. The unassuming Clark shook the great man’s hand in acknowledgement and smiled politely.

When the lift reached his floor, Pele walked away with a final wave. The doors closed and Clark turned to Provan – the winger’s jaw still pinned to the floor – and asked straight-faced, “Who the hell was that?”

A football anorak, he had an encyclopedic memory for dates, opponents and games. Wagging a finger in the air, he would recall the name of a guy he marked in 1964 as if it was yesterday. If he failed to recognise Pele, it was a first.

Marink Reedijk lays down Aberdeen challenge to Hibs team after Hearts win It pushes you forward – Jacob Murrell feeling fuelled by Falkirk fan fervour

Confirming the veracity of the story, his granddaughter tells The Fixture: “My mum always told me that lift story was true. He used to laugh about it.” Most people did, to be fair.

For the best part of six decades, Clark served Celtic as a player, coach, assistant manager, long-standing kit man and club ambassador. Willie Maley might be the only man in Celtic’s history to give more years of his life to the club.

A central defender who formed a formidable partnership with Billy McNeill, he was just five foot eight and referred to almost everyone he met as “big man”. Yet, when he passed away, it felt like the Scottish game had lost a gentle giant.

A winner of four league titles, four League Cups and three Scottish Cups, his crowning glory was Lisbon 1967 when Celtic were crowned champions of Europe.

The 60th anniversary of that Inter Milan victory falls next May, with Jim Craig, Bobby Lennox and Willie Wallace the only Lions still alive to mark the occasion. Craig spoke in these pages of his own battle with Alzheimer’s this year and all three

Lions face health challenges likely to limit their involvement in the celebrations.

For the Clark family, last year’s loss will only add to the poignancy and, in a quest to preserve his memory, the John Clark Legacy Trust has been established to raise funds for a statue in his honour.

A special charity walk is scheduled for three stages on Saturday, November 21. The first stage will cover Chapelhall to Billy McNeill’s statue in Bellshill. The second will move to Jimmy Johnstone’s plinth in Viewpark. The final leg will see those taking part walk to Celtic Park.

“Grandad would have said, ‘I don’t want people to put themselves out’.

“He would say, ‘You don’t need to do that’.

“He would have thought there were more remarkable people who deserved it more than him…”

Celtic supporters would disagree with that sentiment. Signing for the club at the age of 17, Clark’s first appearance came at Arbroath’s Gayfield in 1959 and his first goal in a Scottish Cup replay at Hibernian two years later. Between April of 1965 and September ’67 he turned out in 140 consecutive matches with no injuries, no squad rotation. If he was fit, he played.

Where other members of Jock Stein’s greatest team were natural extroverts who revelled in wine, women and song, Clark was more considered; an unassuming man with a dry sense of humour who was uncomfortable in the spotlight.

“He was always a very hands-on grandad,” adds Clare. “He went under the radar. He wouldn’t do anything to be big or flashy.

“I remember the day he unfurled the league flag at Parkhead [in 2015] and he was nervous because he didn’t know how people would react to him doing it. He was humble like that.”

A Parkhead regular from the age of three, a matchday ticket would usually come with a £10 or £20 note attached without fuss or ceremony.

“It was always just the small gestures he preferred. We high fived on Christmas Day because we were never a touchy-feely family. But that was how he was, undemonstrative.

“He was quietly there in the background if you needed anything and he was one of the kindest and most patient people. So much so that I probably had him wrapped around my finger at times.”

Clark’s own father, John senior, was a railway engineer who died in an accident in Watford when his son was just 10.

Thrust into the role of bread-winner for his mother and siblings, a local farmer allowed him to sell eggs and potatoes to make ends meet.

“During the 50th anniversary celebrations for the Lisbon Lions, the BBC did a documentary and that was the first time we as a family had really heard my grandad talk about the loss of his father,” said Clare.

“It had probably affected him more than he wanted to say. But I don’t know if he would have been the man he was without going through those hardships.

“His siblings Michael, Maureen and Margaret are still here and they idolised him because he had to stand up and do things he didn’t want to do.

“Aunt Margaret has no memory of her dad. And granddad kind of filled that role for her. He always wanted to do the best for his family.”

John Clark in action for Celtic (Image: Colorsport / Shutterstock)

Clark actually had two families in life. The first was his wife Eileen, children Martin and Marie and their three grandchildren. The other were the band of brothers famously assembled from within a 30-mile radius of Glasgow to become the first British winners of the European Cup.

There are times, now, when the current team’s performances and results in UEFA club competitions feel like an affront to the memory of the halcyon days. While Thursday’s win over Besiktas avoided a record run of five straight defeats in Europe, the 60th anniversary will serve as a stark reminder of how far standards have fallen.

“It will be hard next year for a number of reasons,” says Clare. “It probably will be the last big anniversary with any of the Lions there.

“They are getting older and there is a personal side to that. We are really close with the family of Bobby Lennox, one of the last living lions.

“When grandad was alive, he would speak to Bobby every day. During Covid they would be on the phone a couple of times a day, it was the thing that kept them going.

“You would hear grandad telling Bobby to make sure he got out and got his steps in round the garden or discussing a game on the TV.

“They were like brothers actually. And we know the McNeill family well, because we were all in Aberdeen together. And it’s sad there are not many Lions left now.

“This 60th anniversary will be very different from the 50th, that’s for sure.”

Approached by North Lanarkshire Council last year, the John Clark Legacy Trust is not the first established to raise money for a Lisbon Lions statue. It is the most recent.

Jim Goodwin says Dundee Utd are eager to keep momentum going against Motherwell Celtic's 'Che Guevaras' should show their fellow fans some respect at this year's AGM

“We want to get the statue in Chapelhall, the same way as Billy [McNeill] has one in Bellshill, Bobby [Lennox] has one in Saltcoats and Tommy [Gemmell] has one in Craigneuk,” said Clare.

The estimated cost of the memorial will be £120,000, with council grants and a series of fundraising events assisting the cause. Roughly 21 kilometres, the charity walk is expected to take five hours and any additional money raised will be put to use in the Chapelhall community.

“We want to carry on pursuing the issues that grandad valued and he really did value the people of Chapelhall,” added Clare.

“Everyone knew him even though he hadn’t lived there for 40 years.

“In this day and age, with the cost of living and putting children through football training every week, kids who are not going to be the next Celtic or Rangers stars still deserve the opportunity to play the game.

“Our plan is to work with local schools and teams to help fund their programmes to get as many young players as possible involved in the game. I think that’s what granddad would have wanted.”

For details of how to donate to the John Clark Legacy Trust email: johnclarklegacytrust@gmail.com

#2032. DC United vs New York City FC - prediction, team news, lineups

By Adepoju Marvellous | 05 Nov 2026 23:38, Last updated: 05 Nov 2026 23:44

DC United and New York City FC bring the curtain down on their respective 2026 Major League Soccer campaigns with Saturday's clash at Audi Field.

With playoff football out of reach for both sides, there is little at stake, but the chance to finish the regular season on a high should ensure a respectable level of intent.

After reaching the postseason in each of the last two years, New York City have only themselves to blame for missing out this term, following a dismal run of just two wins from 15 outings since returning from Leagues Cup duty.

Pascal Jansen’s men would have gone into their season finale still in playoff contention with a win over Montreal - a result they looked set to secure thanks to Andres Perea’s opener - before Daniel Rios stunned Citi Field with a 91st-minute equaliser.

That was the 12th of 45 goals conceded by the Pigeons between the 75th minute and full time, a lack of late-game focus that Jansen must address next season, should he remain in charge.

While largely inconsequential, a win over DC United could marginally bolster the 57-year-old’s prospects of staying in the dugout, but his record against Saturday’s opposite number is poor, with two defeats from their previous two managerial head-to-heads.

Having lost each of the last two editions - one to this weekend’s opponents - NYCFC’s recent record in season finales is underwhelming as this weekend’s visitors seek to hand DC United a first defeat in five meetings.

As DC United prepare to close out their 2026 MLS campaign, they will hope never to endure another season as disappointing as this one, which easily ranks among the worst in the club’s history since returning to the top flight in 2008.

February’s 1-0 triumph over Philadelphia Union was expected to signal the start of something special for Rene Weiler’s men, but they have since suffered a downward spiral - not quite as severe as last season’s bottom-place finish in the Eastern Conference, but still disappointing.

Saturday’s 3-0 defeat to Columbus Crew marked a fifth consecutive loss and a 14th in 33 matches for Rene Weiler’s side, who have managed just seven wins this term, the second-fewest in the division, ahead of only Montreal’s tally of six.

With just 39 goals scored, the Eagles have been largely ineffective at the top end of the pitch despite Tai Baribo’s impressive return of 16 goals in 25 matches, without which things would have looked much worse from an attacking perspective.

Weiler’s 0.95 points per game in charge of DC United is his lowest average across all clubs managed since 2019. While his position appears safe for now, the Swiss coach will already be planning a turnaround next season, and avoiding defeat on Saturday would at least offer a positive note to end an otherwise disastrous campaign.

Hosei Kijima and Louis Munteanu remain sidelined with leg injuries, while Gabriel Segal is unavailable for DC United due to an ankle problem.

First-choice goalkeeper Sean Johnson (knee) remains out, so Alex Bono should continue between the posts.

Top scorer Tai Baribo will not have the chance to add to his 16 goals due to a hip problem, rounding out the hosts’ list of absentees alongside Kye Rowles, who misses out through suspension.

New York City’s Australian duo Kai Trewin and Aiden O’Neill are out with ankle injuries, while fellow midfielder Maxi Moralez (knee) continues his spell on the treatment table.

Nineteen-year-old Drew Baiera has seen his debut campaign disrupted by injuries and will not feature this weekend, joining Arnau Farnos (leg) and Alonso Martinez (thigh) on the sidelines.

#2031. Nacional vs Academico de Viseu - prediction, team news, lineups

By Adeyeye Oluwapelumi | 05 Nov 2026 23:44

Academico de Viseu will be out to secure their seventh league victory on the trot when they travel to Estadio da Madeira on Saturday to face a Nacional side still searching for stability following another managerial change.

The visitors sit sixth in the Liga Portugal table, just below the continental places on goal difference, while that same metric has the hosts 15th and only just clear of the relegation zone.

Nacional will hope that their third managerial appointment of the season can provide the stability needed to climb away from the lower reaches of the table following the arrival of Joao Henriques on October 26, after Alexandre Santos' brief spell in charge.

Santos suffered defeat in all four of his matches at the helm, including a shock Taca de Portugal exit to lower-league Sanjoanense, before Under-19s manager Bruno Abreu took charge and guided the side to a 1-0 victory over Braga, ending their six-match losing run in the league.

However, Henriques was unable to build on that result in his first game in charge, with the Alvinegros suffering a narrow 1-0 defeat away to Arouca, leaving the Funchal outfit with just two wins from their opening 10 Primeira Liga fixtures (D1, L7).

Both victories have come at Estadio da Madeira, offering some encouragement ahead of Saturday's encounter, knowing that taking maximum points at the weekend could hinge on defensive solidity, given their successes this term only came in games they kept clean sheets.

Supporters of the Alvinegros can also take some comfort from their side's record against Viseu in Funchal, having won three of the previous five meetings between the clubs (D1, L1) there, although their most recent home encounter ended in a 1-1 draw in Liga 2 in March 2024.

Viseu, meanwhile, have enjoyed an impressive start to life back in the top flight after failing to win any of their opening four fixtures, although an encouraging draw away to Benfica on matchday one offered an early indication of their potential.

Bruno Pinheiro's side have since recorded victories in each of their last six league matches, beating Gil Vicente, Vitoria de Guimaraes, Estrela Amadora, Estoril Praia and Sporting Lisbon before securing a 2-1 comeback triumph over Rio Ave last weekend.

That result means Academico have scored exactly twice in each of their last five top-flight outings, taking their league tally to 15 goals, with only the traditional big three of Porto (23), Benfica (27) and Sporting (23) finding the net more often.

Viseu have also alternated between league victories and cup defeats across their last four matches in all competitions, having been eliminated from the Taca de Portugal by lower-league Fatima before suffering Taca da Liga disappointment against Porto.

#2029. From Hibs casual to a sold-out Hydro - the incredible story of bare-knuckle boxing's Leith Warrior

The hands might tell a story although Lewis Knox will hope they know when to stop blabbing. After all, he doesn't want his tools of the trade to betray him.

These fists helped him survive on Leith’s mean streets. As a former Hibs casual, he once used them to defend his club’s honour.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

In a more legitimate context, one less likely to interest the authorities, they are crucial for his current job installing sofas up and down the country. And more pressingly, in Glasgow on Saturday, these hands will be used as weapons with the aim of drawing blood.

“All legal and above board,” Knox clarifies. Welcome to the world of “BKFC”, which stands for Bare Knuckle Fighting Championship. The promotion, co-owned by controversial UFC star Conor McGregor, hits Scotland for the first time this weekend.

Only the All Blacks’ visit to Murrayfield, Celtic v Kilmarnock and possibly Aberdeen v Hibs will attract a bigger crowd in a sporting context.

Still, it’s guaranteed none of those involved in these fixtures will have spent the start of this week lugging sofas up and down stairwells. “I install them into houses from Berwick-Upon-Tweed to near enough Stonehaven," says Knox. "12-hour shifts, 7 am to 7 pm. Four days on, four days off. But I am still training every night. As well as being a dad of three."

Even the All Blacks, who have been utilising the gym where Knox has been training under the watchful eye of Ali Thomson, might wince at the thought of this schedule. Thomson describes Knox as a "phenomenon". He complains his own arms are aching from doing pads with the focused fighter in the run-up to this weekend.

"People say things are impossible,” ponders Knox. “But you know if you really want it? Things can be done. My mum, my dad, my family. They all support me. Everyone is tuned into it. They all try to help out. This is not an overnight thing, this has been three years in the making to get to where I am now. I have worked so hard."

He was in Fife as recently as Monday delivering sofas but who knows where he will be this time next year? The bare-knuckle scene is taking off, boosted by McGregor's involvement. "I'd like to turn pro," says Knox, 29. Remember that Hearts fan ridiculed for claiming on camera that he’d be willing to have his hands chopped off if it meant his team winning the league?

Knox loves Hibs. He was thrilled by last weekend’s League Cup semi-final win over Hearts at Hampden, which he watched on TV because he was deep in fight camp. However, he can’t afford to strike any bargain involving the prospect of losing his hands. As a bare-knuckle boxer on the cusp of his biggest ever fight, they are, after his three children, among the most precious things on earth to him.

Perhaps a little Atrixo might be in order. They are battered, bruised and a little disfigured. Hardly surprising really, since they are used to pound his opponents. “Bone on bone,” he says. “There is nothing more raw.” He reports that he hasn't broken his hands in his last three fights. "They are solid, like sledgehammers," he says.

Rather than slathering them with hand cream, Knox is considering the old fighters’ trick of sticking his hands into a bucket of sand – or rice. “It strengthens up the skin,” he says.

He broke two knuckles in his very first (official) bare-knuckle fight three years ago this month. Slightly horrifyingly, these knuckles now appear to have disappeared completely. “Yeah, disintegrated,” he says. “Two knuckles have gone, one has dipped (into the hand). As for my pinkie, I can’t stretch it out."

Knox demonstrates this inability to extend his little finger in the café where we are sitting. The Leith Warrior, as he’s known, has ordered a flat white with a shot of caramel (there was still plenty of time to make the required fighting weight of 66 kgs). If not for the damage to his hands, he seems incredibly unwarrior-like.

Softly spoken and trim, almost delicate-looking, the tattoos extending past his collar line on his neck are perhaps the main evidence of a life lived on the edge.

“I always wanted tattoos,” he says. As one suspects is the case with many people, he first succumbed to the needle and ink on holiday in Magaluf.

“A star on my chest and a Hibs tattoo on the back of my calf,” he says. “I thought I had to get serious ones after that. Ones devoted to my gran and my grandad, who both played huge parts in my life from a young age. I also have a gladiator on my arm and neck tattoos…It has become part of the job!”

As for the colours he sports when competing in the circular four-rope ring, which is designed to encourage fast-paced bouts, it wasn’t up for discussion. “Green and white, I always represent where I am from,” he says. “And a Hibs badge on my shorts. I am never not representing Leith.

“I grew up in Leith, a lot of gang culture, an environment of violence as a young boy,” he continues. “You had to be streetwise from a young age I suppose. Leith has its good and bad sides. For me, it’s one of the best places in the world. But it can be one of the worst places in the world.

"Knife crime, drugs. It’s a mix of cultures, backgrounds. I grew up in all of that. But I was never ultra-violent.”

His mother, Niki, once ran the Junction bar. Knox enjoys an obvious status in the area. A taxi driver beeps his horn as soon as he steps out of the door of our meeting place on Easter Road. Cross Knoxy and you cross Leith.

He knows people, Irvine Welsh included. The author – a more than decent boxer himself - has been mentoring Knox before his featherweight division fight against Tommy “Chaos” Carus from Liverpool at the OVO Hydro on Saturday night. Welsh has already featured in an Instagram video promoting Knox’s fight, playing the role of his manager.

“Oi, Knoxy!” he calls out after taking a phone call. “Get your dancing shoes on! We’ve got ourselves a pagger.”

Knox v Carus, or the Leith Warrior v Chaos, or indeed Scotland v England, is the third fight of 11 on a bill topped by Sean Weir’s light heavyweight title bout with Leigh Cohoon, a late stand-in for Irishman Conor ‘Da Crook’ Cooke.

Cooke’s team cited concerns about the venue layout and ticketing arrangements for their withdrawal. Some have interpreted this as another way of saying they were worried sectarian/football-related hooliganism – Weir was once a member of the Rangers Riot Crew casuals group - could flare.

Almost 11,000 are expected to converge on the Hydro for the event. BKFC is dedicated to “fighter safety”. According to their official bumph, the organisation prides itself in being “the truest form of bare-knuckle fighting”. Fighters are not allowed to wrap their hands to within one inch of the knuckle. This weekend’s spectacle is the first legally sanctioned and regulated bare knuckle event in Scotland.

For the uninitiated, the fights last for five two-minute rounds. If there isn’t a knockout, it tends to be fairly obvious who’s won.

“Cuts,” says Knox. “It comes down to facial damage. Because in boxing or any gloved fight, you can punch them ten times with a glove and not make a mark, you can punch them once with a bare knuckle and split someone’s head open.

“It is about getting as much of that in in a short period of time. The first punch usually sets the tone for the fight. It depends on where you catch him, I suppose. It is all about just getting in there and being horrible.”

It’s easy to question the ethics of unpadded pugilism. However, defenders of this ancient and previously underground practice insist it’s a safer, more honest form of boxing. "It is better for the brain, much better," claims Knox. "In boxing you get the double shock with the glove – boom, boom. It rattles the brain. You don’t see the damage facially necessarily. With bare knuckle, bone is hitting bone. That’s it. The facial damage will be shown. Internally your brain is not getting rattled for 12 rounds.

“It is five rounds of two minutes. If you last that, although you might get a few cuts, your brain is fine. To me, my brain feels fine! In my 50s and 60s I will still have a functional brain. I might have a few scars and a few missing teeth but I move pretty well (to avoid the punches). My nose is still straight...”

Inside the ring might be a veritable haven as the evening hots up on Saturday. “It is like any combat sport,” says Knox. “The crowd can be unpredictable. A bit like a football crowd. I just hope that because this event is so big for Scotland and so big for the bare-knuckle scene and for lads like myself that nothing serious kicks off. There will be some ‘characters’ there, you always get the odd person. You get that anywhere.”

Knox anticipates an unholy commotion when the first bars of Born Slippy strike up. The Underworld track is his walk on song, unsurprisingly given the Trainspotting connotations. Sunshine on Leith just wouldn’t do it in this context. Fine for after last weekend’s win for Hibs at Hampden against Hearts, but perhaps a little too plaintive, a little too pretty, for a night of good-to-honest testosterone-fuelled violence.

As much as the Easter Road club might wish otherwise, a line – if admittedly indirect - can be drawn between Hibs and Knox’s prowess in the ring.

“Before I got into bare knuckle, I boxed," he says. "But I was also fighting in football as well. I grew up in a place where there was a lot of gang culture, an environment of violence as a young boy. You had to be streetwise from a young age I suppose.”

He ran with the Capital City Service – Hibs casuals – from 17-years-old onwards. “I found it attractive,” he says. “It was something I felt I was missing: being part of a brotherhood, a group.”

The casuals scene, including rival groups such as ASC (Aberdeen Soccer Casuals) and Dundee Utility, seems to belong to another era of Scottish football. But the fights still happen, just further away from stadiums.

“Anywhere there isn’t cameras,” he says. “Back in the 80s and most of the 90s, you had groups of a hundred plus. Since TV took over, groups became smaller, more confined, more secret. You had to move with the times I suppose. You couldn’t wander around in groups of hundreds, you’d be seen by all the cameras.”

It became violence by appointment. “You’d phone and say: ‘Meet you there’. A set meet. Sometimes nothing would ever happen. You’d phone all day and nothing would happen. But you’d still have that day out with your mates.”

The arrangements could be painstaking. “It was all planned out. You needed management skills! A lot went into it. You didn’t just turn up and fight. What time were we fighting, what time were the trains, what pubs to go to? It was a lot of work. I could probably pass a management course now quite easily!”

Unlike some, Knox would always endeavour to go the game. He was and remains a football fan and played at a decent level. His first ambition was to be a professional footballer. He played for Hawick Royal Albert and Coldstream in the East of Scotland league – on the wing, wing-back or full-back and then, latterly, as a sweeper with a reputation for never shirking a tackle.

“I was still involved in the casuals scene, still attracted to it,” he says. “It was not all about violence. It was about being with your mates. We dressed the same, liked the same music. Away days having a laugh. It wasn’t all about fighting.”

But some of it undoubtedly was. He remembers once playing in a Scottish Junior Cup tie for Newcraighall, which had kicked off early. “I then went home and got changed before a fight with Raith Rovers, who were playing a Scottish Cup tie against Hibs,” he says.

“Everyone has got a bit older now. The scene has changed. Six guys v six guys, in a forest somewhere. Last team standing wins. To me that’s not football casuals, because you are away from everything.”

“I am not saying football violence is good,” he says. “But there’s so much more to it. It’s guys looking forward to being with their mates, they maybe need that at the end of the week. It’s a release. It acts as therapy for some people.”

The message is: don’t diss what you’ve never tried. The same could apply to bare-knuckle boxing, which is now edging into the mainstream to the extent that this weekend’s extravaganza has been advertised on the side of buses.

Maybe an invite onto the pitch at Hibs before a game might be forthcoming for Knox – it ought to be if he prevails this weekend, which would mean he is the No. 1 contender for the UK featherweight bare-knuckle title.

His ultimate dream is one likely to give Edinburgh city fathers pause. “My goal, my dream fight, if it wasn't Easter Road, would be on the castle esplanade,” he says. “Outdoors, in the summer. It would have a gladiatorial feel about it, you know? That would just be amazing.”

#2028. Preston North End vs Southampton - prediction, team news, lineups

By Ben Sully | 05 Nov 2026 23:59, Last updated: 07 Nov 2026 11:10

Southampton will look to extend their six-game unbeaten run when they travel to Deepdale for Saturday’s clash with Preston North End.

The Saints are currently operating in seventh spot in the Championship standings, while PNE are propping up the table after taking just five points from their 14 matches.

Preston boss Graham Alexander has failed to spark an upturn in fortunes since being named as Paul Heckingbottom’s successor at the end of September.

Alexander has lost five of his six matches in charge (D1), including a 2-0 defeat in last Saturday’s away clash against Stoke City.

PNE experienced more disappointment in midweek, despite taking an early lead in their home meeting with Sheffield United.

Sydie Peck’s 19-minute hat-trick left Preston trailing by two goals at half time, and while Callum Lang pulled a goal back in the 77th minute, PNE ultimately failed to find an equaliser as they fell to their 11th Championship defeat of the season.

As a result of their struggles, Preston are already nine points adrift from safety, leaving them with a mountain to climb if they are to extend their 12-season stay in the second tier.

Alexander will be aware that his team needs to improve significantly in both boxes, as Preston currently have the league’s worst defensive record with 30 goals conceded and are among the division’s lowest scorers with just 12 goals to their name.

In contrast to their hosts, Southampton have proven to be a tough team to beat this term, having won eight, drawn four and lost just two of their 14 Championship matches.

In fact, Tonda Eckert's side have put together a six-game unbeaten run since suffering their most recent defeat in an away clash against Wrexham on September 19.

Samuel Edozie made sure Southampton extended that unbeaten streak in Tuesday’s meeting with West Bromwich Albion, netting a 53rd-minute equaliser to cancel out Isaac Price’s penalty at The Hawthorns.

The promotion hopefuls, who were deducted four points at the start of the season, are currently two points clear of Sheffield United in ninth position and three points adrift of second-placed Wolverhampton Wanderers.

They will certainly fancy their chances of adding three points to their tally against a struggling Preston side, especially as they have won on two of their previous three visits to Deepdale, including a 3-1 victory in May.

That said, they have struggled for consistency on their travels, having won two, drawn three and lost two of their seven away league games this season.

Preston are still having to contend without the services of Harry Clarke, Lewis Gibson, Liam Gibbs and Ali McCann.

Johnny Kenny has been added to the injury list after he was forced off in the 12th minute against Sheffield United due to a hamstring problem.

Midfielder Leo Leroy will miss Saturday’s game through suspension after collecting his fifth yellow card of the season in the midweek defeat.

As for the visitors, midfielder Caspar Jandar will have to be assessed after sitting out the last two games with a muscular injury.

Southampton’s top scorer Cyle Larin is another fitness concern, having been forced to miss the last three games with a hamstring problem.

Eckert, meanwhile, is confident Leo Scienza will be ready to feature at Deepdale after being ruled out for the midweek draw with West Brom.

Preston North End possible starting lineup:

Iversen; Offiah, Lindsay, Hughes; Mills, Potts, Thompson, Wiley; Lang, Devine; Erabi

Peretz; Bree, Stephens, Schlotterbeck, Manning; Ward-Prowse, Downes; Matsuki, Azaz, Scienza; Dobbin

While Southampton have tended to save their best performances for St Mary's, they will view Saturday's contest as a great opportunity to claim their third away win of the Championship season.

With the Saints currently the league's third-highest scorers, we ultimately believe they will be too strong for a Preston side with the worst defensive record in the second tier.

The 33-year-old started his career at Liverpool, coming through the youth ranks to make two senior appearances, before spells at Huddersfield, Wolves, Everton, Leicester, Wrexham and then a loan stint with Charlton last season.

Coady, who captained Wolves and made 317 appearances for the Molineux club, admitted in an emotional post on Instagram it was a tough decision, but which came at the right time.

“Eight clubs, 503 appearances, two promotions, a World Cup and a Euros, 10 England caps, football is my life, it always has been, but everything at some point always comes to an end,” he said.

“I never ever thought playing for Wolves in Europe or going with England to a World Cup this day would come, but honestly, the last couple of years have been tough, not playing as much as I would have liked I have struggled with, as I live for playing footie.

“The truth is I am ready now. I have given football everything and I will continue to do so in my next chapter.”

Coady won 10 senior caps for England and went to the Euro 2020 and World Cup 2022 finals.

Meanwhile, Championship strugglers Preston have signed former Rangers midfielder Greg Docherty on a deal to the end of the season.

The 30-year-old midfielder, who has previously played for Hibs among others, was a free agent after leaving Charlton in the summer and has been training with Preston for the past two weeks, playing for their under-21s in a 1-0 Premier League Cup win over Fleetwood.

Preston boss Graham Alexander, seeking to guide North End off the foot of the table, said: “We’re really pleased to bring Greg in. He’s been a captain, won promotions and knows the game inside out.

“Greg’s vocal, fit and motivated, which are all the key things you look for in a professional footballer. He has settled into the group really quickly and has a real willingness to show what he can do.”

#2026. Project 2035 sounds good but Scottish women’s football needs more than bold promises

A hefty dose of cynicism is always healthy whenever a politician turns up to kick a ball about with a group of kids for the cameras.

John Swinney got to work on his keepie-uppie skills this week at Easter Road as Project 2035 was rolled out in an initiative between the Scottish government and the SFA, among others, with the long-term ambitions of the project comfortably ticking the “ambitious in outlook” box.

It would be hard to find fault with the bold objectives that have been set for the next decade.

There were the immediate headline takeaways; doubling the number of registered female players in the country and quadrupling attendances at matches jumped out. Key, too, is regular qualification for major tournaments – and making an impact when qualification has been secured.

In terms of a manifesto that is exciting and visionary, there was much to be pleased about. But, as ever, the proof will be in the pudding. And when it comes to past behaviours predicting future outcomes, it would have to be said Scotland have excelled at taskforces and not quite so much at outcomes.

The initial outlay from the government is £250,000 for this year. That will cover the first step of their contribution but across the remaining terms until 2035 – by which time Scotland will hope to be co-hosts at the Women’s World Cup – the reality is that if those ambitions are to come to fruition, then pockets will need to be pretty deep.

It will take a lot of work and a lot of joined-up thinking across the board but the key to it all, as ever, is money.

The reality just now is this is a Scotland national team who have not qualified for a major tournament since 2019. There has been a regression in the SWPL both in terms of attendances, media exposure, quality and standard of players.

The league itself is split in terms of those who can afford to offer full-time professional contracts and those who can pay a tenner a week for expenses. A full-time professional SWPL may well be the first major step towards any quest to take the country to a level where it is fulfilling the objectives that were set out this week.

As it stands, that possibility would seem to be light years away.

It is not all doom and gloom. Scotland coach Melissa Andreatta has injected more than just enthusiasm and positivity into the national set-up. Initial impressions of her impact are positive, as witnessed by an unbeaten Nations League campaign and a return to League A.

Brazil next summer is the big one. Getting past Sweden in a two-legged World Cup play-off final next month would be the biggest result in Scotland’s history. It is fair to say it is a monumental challenge that lies ahead.

Caroline Weir has been shortlisted in successive years for the Ballon d’Or while Erin Cuthbert captains Chelsea in the WSL. Kim Little’s time with the national team has long since passed but that trio provide compelling evidence that Scotland have been able to produce world-class players.

But as the game has developed at a rate of knots elsewhere, it has stagnated in Scotland.

Lessons have to be learned from 2019, from the way that 18,555 fans turned up to wave Scotland off to France for their first World Cup to a collapse in interest and exposure within months. To understand how to get it right, there needs to be an understanding of where it went wrong.

The approach from government bodies to work in tandem with the SFA is sensible. The benefits of women retained in sport, not even at elite level but simply a recreational level, have a huge societal knock-on effect.

But it will need more than platitudes in front of cameras. The real work will be done in the nitty-gritty, day-to-day work. And elevating Scotland to the levels spoken about this week ultimately requires significant investment.

Megan Rapinoe has always been Marmite-like; observers either love her frank outspokenness or find their hackles rising on the back of it.

There are some arguments to suggest a woman with strong opinions she isn’t afraid to share will always invite a backlash. In any case, Rapinoe, so central for so long to such a successful USWNT as she claimed two World Cups and an Olympic goal medal, has been consistent that she sees no issue with trans athletes, a conversation that never seems to be too far from the surface in women’s sport.

Rapinoe’s argument centred on the idea there is no fairness in sport, citing the natural advantages of 7-foot-4-inch basketball player Victor Wembanyama as her example.

The problem with that comparison, however, is it fundamentally misses the point that biological males have a distinct advantage when it comes to competing.

Kelly Clark found herself out of Celtic’s starting line-up across recent weeks. The first Celtic women’s captain to lead the club to a title and the first to take them

into the Champions League, one suspects that finding herself on the bench would have been a sobering experience, and novel given the fact

she has been a mainstay of this Celtic team.

Drafted back into the starting XI, she produced a big goal for Grant Scott’s side on Wednesday night as she gave the Parkhead side a win over Hibs at Meadowbank.

Plenty of life in her yet, it would seem.

Houston arrive on 51 points from 14 wins, nine draws and 10 defeats, and a 3-1 loss at Portland on November 1 dropped them from the top four to fifth, level with St Louis on points but behind on goal difference.

That defeat followed a 1-0 win at Seattle on October 28, Houston’s first road win over the Sounders, courtesy of Lucas Halter’s 26th-minute header from a Mateusz Bogusz corner, his first goal in 20 league appearances this season.

Jonathan Bond made six saves as Seattle outshot Houston 21-2, and the clean sheet was Houston’s 13th of the MLS season, which equals the club record.

The win ended a seven-match winless run in the league that included a 0-0 draw at home to Minnesota United on October 24.

At Portland, Agustin Bouzat’s 71st-minute strike was Houston’s only shot on target, against six for the Timbers, whose goals came from David Da Costa, Kristoffer Velde and Vincent Janssen.

Guilherme was directly involved in 26 of Houston’s 42 league goals before that game, a rate of 61.9%, which helps explain why the Dynamo created so little without him and Hector Herrera, with Guilherme’s 16 goals and 10 assists the best return in the squad.

St Louis also have 51 points from 14 wins, nine draws and 10 defeats, and they hold fourth place on a goal difference of +10 to Houston’s +1.

A 3-0 defeat at Real Salt Lake followed on October 24, with Tomas Ostrak sent off for a second yellow card in the 44th minute, then a 3-2 loss to Portland at Energizer Park on October 28 and a 1-0 loss to San Diego on October 31 through Anders Dreyer’s 38th-minute goal, despite City having 16 shots to 12 and seven on target to three.

Yoann Damet blames fatigue after seven matches in 20 days, a run that included winning the US Open Cup final at Columbus on October 21, where a 0-0 draw became a 5-3 penalty shootout win after Ben Lundt saved the opening spot kick and Daniel Edelman scored the decisive one.

Carlo Holse, signed from Samsunspor for a reported $6m, the most expensive signing in club history, scored a hat-trick inside 21 minutes of the 6-2 win over LA Galaxy on October 11, the second regular-season hat-trick in City’s history.

St Louis have beaten Houston twice in 2026, winning the US Open Cup quarter-final on penalties on May 19 after a 2-2 draw in which Lundt saved Guilherme’s and Herrera’s spot kicks, and the league meeting 2-1 on August 22 through Dante Polvara’s 86th-minute winner after Ibrahim Aliyu’s equaliser, while Marcel Hartel, who scored twice in the cup tie, was sold to Hannover on August 11.

Bond was replaced in the starting lineup during the warm-up at Portland and Jimmy Maurer is out with a back injury, so Blake Gillingham started and made three saves.

Guilherme and Herrera both missed the Portland game and neither has been confirmed for Saturday, while Marcelo Saracchi remains out.

Franco Negri was substituted in the 36th minute at Portland and replaced by Duane Holmes, Felipe Andrade returned from injury off the bench, and Agustin Resch has been back in the defence alongside Halter since the Seattle game.

Alexandru Matan, who has missed the last three league matches with a lower-leg injury, was also back in training on Tuesday and could be limited to a place on the bench.

Ostrak came off the bench against San Diego after his red card at Salt Lake, Holse was left out of the starting lineup for the Minnesota and Salt Lake defeats, and striker Rafael Navarro, who scored the opener at Minnesota, was ineligible for the Open Cup final.

“Kasper had a brilliant game. That's the life of a striker - you have to be there to take them. His all-round game today was very good. He gave us a platform to play.”

Sunday, August 9, the words of Celtic assistant coach Shaun Maloney after watching striker Kasper Hogh score a 33-minute hat-trick in a 5-1 win over Kilmarnock.

Did you know with a Digital Subscription to The Scotsman, you can get unlimited access to the website including our premium content, as well as benefiting from fewer ads, loyalty rewards and much more.

Hogh had not long arrived at Celtic from Bodo/Glimt for £12 million, a record signing for the Scottish champions. His predatory instincts in Ayrshire led many to believe the Dane was on his way to the golden boot.

Fifteen games on for Celtic, Hogh has not scored a goal since. In fact, his manager Martin O’Neill is yet to see him find the net, as he was recovering from a “small procedure” for the match at Rugby Park.

Maybe the visit of Kilmarnock, who he terrorised on that summer’s afternoon, on Sunday will be the match where Hogh finally finds the net again. That is, of course, if the 25-year-old gets the nod in attack.

Hogh’s star is waning. The 25-year-old has been eclipsed by fellow July signing Camilo Duran, who has netted 13 times this season and clambered off the bench to help Celtic defeat Besiktas on Thursday night. The Colombian did more in his half-hour cameo than Hogh did in double that time. The poor hitman didn’t touch the ball once in the Turkish penalty box in the opening period.

It would be unfair to judge Hogh wholly on his goals, although at £4m per strike so far, that is an expensive outlay. Physical and hard-working, he offers Celtic a focal point. O’Neill was pleased with his performance against Besiktas. “I want centre-forwards to be able to hold it and that is what he did,” said the manager. “He is not Duran, he is not a dribbler. But if he can do this for us against strong opposition it will stand him in good stead.”

Hogh’s belief is bound to be low. How could it not be? He is out of the Denmark squad for the first time in over a year and when he tapped in from an already rescinded free-kick against Besiktas, there was a slightly sarcastic cheer from the home crowd. The misfiring forward is a real talking point.

“I think Thursday night will be good for him,” continued O’Neill. “I said to him that I’m not worried about whether he scores a goal. Of course you want centre-forwards to score and of course centre-forwards live on them. But I said to him that last night I wanted him to be strong and fight when the ball is played up to him. I thought in terms of holding the ball up and bringing people into the game that he did really well.

“Centre-forwards need a goal. But that performance there against European opposition will give him confidence. I don’t know what side we will play him on Sunday. But this lad has scored goals in the Champions League, remember. He will get a confidence boost from last night in terms of doing that part of the game well. But it will be nice for him to score a goal.”

The problem Hogh perhaps had is that O’Neill will turn to Duran more often than not now. “At this minute, he is on fire,” added O’Neill of the South American. “He can play wide right, he has done that. He has played wide left. But centre forward is where he is dynamic.” For now, unlike his strike partner.

#2017. How Iceland tackled its substance abuse crisis with sport and what Scotland can learn

Abler, the software that was launched by former Icelandic handball player Markus Maute nine years ago and is now used by the majority of sporting organisations in his homeland, has made it across the North Atlantic to Scotland.

Aberdeen, Alloa Athletic, Ayr United, Dundee United, Montrose, Stenhousemuir and Stirling Albion are among the growing number of senior clubs here whose academies and community trusts have embraced the bespoke administrative system.

Grassroots outfits like Corstorphine Dynamo, Giffnock Soccer Centre, Jeanfield Swifts, North Merchiston and Vics in the Community, too, have found that many mundane but vital tasks have become far simpler since tapping into the online platform. Who knows where it will all end?

“The entire sports network over here in Iceland runs on our software and app now,” said Maute. “It has even grown outside the realm of sport. I think something like 75 per cent of people here are on Abler in some capacity. Even God is on it these days. The churches here organise their services using it as well.”

Could Scotland address some of its societal problems by following Iceland's innovative approach to youth sport as well? Maute believes there would be considerable benefits.

He is still grateful for the support which he received on a daily basis at his local handball club in Reykjavik when he was a young boy growing up in a single-parent family back in the 1980s and 1990s.

The encouragement and expert advice he was given enabled him to fulfil his childhood dream and play the game professionally when he left school; he turned out for HSG Dusseldorf in the German Bundesliga for two seasons during the early 2000s.

Yet the former left back saw first-hand just how seismic an impact increased government funding for sport had on the wider population in Iceland, not just those who, like him, excelled in their chosen pastime, during his formative years.

Alarming rates of drinking, smoking and drug use among adolescents prompted politicians at national and regional level to develop and roll out a groundbreaking prevention model which has attracted attention around the world.

Instead of investing in awareness campaigns, higher policing levels and more robust border controls, they put money into organised leisure and sport, facilitated stronger parental involvement and restricted access to alcohol and tobacco. The results have been nothing short of remarkable.

“In the late 1980s and early 1990s there was a substance abuse crisis in Iceland among teenagers,” said Maute. “In 1998, 42 per cent of Icelandic 15 and 16-year-olds reported having been drunk in the previous 30 days, 23 per cent had smoked daily and 17 per cent had used cannabis. The youth of the country was not in a good place.

A kid plays football on a pitch in Iceland (Image: Promotional)

“So the politicians came together and decided they needed to find something else for youngsters to do. They did a really good thing for once - they started to invest in sport. They built very good infrastructure for sports clubs in all of their municipalities. Suddenly, everyone had excellent, accessible facilities. That was key to the turnaround.

“Clubs here received a lot of financial support. The government built the infrastructure and then gifted the facilities to them so they didn't have to fund the construction of a new pitch, changing rooms, or a stand. Those things can be a huge burden on clubs.

“The policy worked. Clubs became like second homes for kids. We hung out there before practice and after practice when I was growing up. I was lucky enough to have great coaches who taught me good values and life skills through sport as well as how to play handball and football.

“A lot of money was put into coach education as well. There are not that many professional coaches in Iceland, but they do get compensated for their time. There are also full-time staff who run clubs now. The set-ups are far more professional and everything is subsidised.

“The municipalities also give parents financial incentives to get their kids involved. For example, I get around £500 a year to use towards my son playing sport or getting involved in music. The money I receive is substantial and definitely makes a big difference.

“It costs around £800 or £900 a year for my 12-year-old boy to play football. But he trains four times a week with a UEFA-qualified coach and he plays games on top of that. It is definitely good value for money.”

Since reaching the quarter-finals of Euro 2016 and qualifying for Russia 2018 – incredible achievements for a country which had a population of just 335,000 people at that time – the Iceland national football team has struggled.

They have many excellent players who ply their trade in the Bundesliga, Eredivisie, La Liga, Ligue 1, Premier League and Serie A. But they failed to reach the Euro 2020, Qatar 2022, Euro 2024 and World Cup 2026 finals.

The focus in the youth game, though, is very much on participation.

“The whole sport system is built around community clubs which are accessible to everyone,” said Maute. “The beauty of it is that it is open to all. Yes, it develops all our best athletes and all of our top footballers. But everyone comes through the same grassroots system.

“Any kid can play. If you have a boy who has never played football and your area has the best football team in the country at his age group then he will still be welcomed with open arms and he will still train alongside the best players.

“People in Iceland understand the important impact this has had in preventing anti-social behaviour. In my neighbourhood, something like 90 per cent of kids who are aged between six and 16 participate in organised sports at their local club. The substance abuse problem which was once so bad has changed enormously.”

Indeed it has. Official figures show that between 1998 and 2018 the proportion of 15 and 16-year-olds in Iceland who reported having been drunk in the previous 30 days fell from 42 per cent to five per cent, daily smoking fell from 23 per cent to three per cent and cannabis use fell from 17 per cent to five per cent.

Kids play football at a community club in Iceland (Image: Promotional)

For Maute and many of his compatriots, the millions which have been pumped into sport have been extremely well spent.

“When kids play sport they get integrated into society,” he said. “They are more likely to get a better job, pay higher taxes, use the healthcare system less and rely on income support and benefits less.”

Maute has been championing the merits of the Abler software to sports clubs, youth organisations, charities and governing bodies across Europe for some time now and has been struck by how differently other countries, including Scotland, deal with their young people and tackle alcohol and drug abuse issues.

“What I like most about the Icelandic system is that nobody has to do trials in order to get into a team,” he said. “That is a very good thing. Even if you’re not an elite-level player, you can still take part. So kids who maybe develop a little slower physically, who might be late bloomers, are not discriminated against.

“I would say that 90 per cent of the boys who are in my son’s class at school take part in his football and handball training. You remain in your friendship circle even if you are an elite guy. Don’t get me wrong, it is still a serious environment where a good player can progress. But you form connections which last a lifetime.

“The community clubs are also in close proximity to the schools. In other countries it can sometimes take a kid an hour to get to training. If they are any good, they are invariably whisked away to another club to play with other promising players and are taken out of their friendship group.

“Putting kids into a professional environment too early is the worst thing you can do in my opinion. Studies have been done which show that if sport becomes too serious too early it puts kids at risk of burnout. Their interest in sport can often fizzle out when they are as young as 12 if they are taken away by an academy.”

The Scottish government continues to wrestle with significant public-health challenges which affect both young people and the wider population.

Concerning Public Health Scotland figures which were released in December showed that 24 per cent of Primary One children were at risk of being overweight or obese in the 2024/25 school year.

The same body revealed in January that there were 29,430 hospital admissions for “conditions wholly attributable to alcohol” during the 2024/25 financial year. National Records of Scotland confirmed that 1,133 drug use deaths were registered here in 2025.

It is overly simplistic to suggest these complex issues can be tackled by allocating increased funding to youth football teams. Still, MSPs at Holyrood and MPs at Westminster could learn much if they studied the success which Iceland has enjoyed through its internationally renowned prevention model.

“I don’t want to comment on how Scottish people should run their country,” said Maute. “But what I would say is that I believe in the Icelandic sports model and the Icelandic methodology. Look at what it has done to our substance abuse issues. The evidence is there.

Markus Maute of Abler (Image: Promottional)

“I have lived it myself. My upbringing would have been completely different without my local sports club. It made me what I am today and it has done the same for so many other kids.

“The government has had to invest for it to work. The infrastructure has been expensive. Good coaches have to be able to make a living out of sport or at least be paid. You can’t depend on volunteers. But when they put money in they know they can get it back later many times over. The numbers prove it.

“More often than not individuals who come through the system will get a job, will pay taxes, will know how to take care of themselves, will understand how to bounce back from adversity when things are not going so well in life.

“I am a great believer in this. I feel we're only scratching the surface of how the life-developing power of sport can be harnessed too. I think it will become even more important in future because so much communication is digital now and sport is one of the last places where kids can come together and connect.”

He added, “I grew up without a father and was very fortunate to have good sports clubs in my neighbourhood during my childhood. I spent most of my time in and around them. The coaches there became my father figures. They gave me a sense of belonging.

“As my business career progressed, I developed ideas about how to improve sport further in Iceland. I said, ‘Do you know what? I'm going to go and talk about my ideas to all the people I respect who are involved in the system because I believe in it a lot.’ They thought my ideas were great so I quit my job and went all in.

“I thought we needed to amplify the life-developing power of sports. Sport is such a powerful tool because kids are so emotionally invested in it. They listen more to their coach than they do their teacher.

“Abler helps to create a better working environment for everyone who is involved in sport so more time and more energy can be put into what really matters: developing good people and great athletes.”

#2013. How Amorim engineered a derby masterclass: Tactical analysis of AC Milan 3-1 Inter

AC Milan tasted derby delight for the fourth time in a row as they dismantled Inter in the first half to take the bragging rights.

It did not take long for Milan to go ahead as Christian Pulisic rose highest to nod in a Diego Moreira cross, and just a few minutes later Adrien Rabiot was on hand to finish off a nicely worked set-piece routine to make it 2-0.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Alessandro Bastoni scored from a corner to make it a one-goal game once again, but then Moreira’s free-kick re-established the two-goal lead and that would be enough to see the Rossoneri home after a more controlled secnd half.

It marked a fourth straight win for Milan against the Nerazzurri and it reduces the gap to the city rivals back down to four points. Below is the tactical breakdown from Rohit Rajeev.

Ruben Amorim chose to make six changes from the team that lost to Bologna on Wednesday night, with Mario Gila, Sankhoun Diawara, Luka Modric, Adrien Rabiot, Diego Moreira and Christian Pulisic all getting the nod.

Milan started with a 4-4-1-1 formation, with Gila, Moreira and Rabiot returning to the starting XI. However, the structure was far from rigid, frequently shifting between a 4-2-3-1 and a 3-4-2-1. Much of this positional fluidity was dictated by the movements of two players in particular: Diawara and Rabiot.

Milan adopted a 3-4-2-1 structure in possession, using a one-up, one-down mechanism to maintain balance in their build-up.

When both Gila and Diawara pushed forward, Modrić dropped into the defensive line to preserve a back three. This ensured Milan always had three players providing rest defence and protection against counter-attacks.

This was one of the key differences between Amorim and Xabi Alonso’s approach at Chelsea. Alonso was more comfortable leaving just two players at the back, allowing Acheampong to advance and accepting the increased risk of counter-attacks.

Chivu was without his captain and leading goalscorer Lautaro Martínez, while also having one eye on Tuesday’s fixture against Feyenoord. He therefore experimented with a 3-4-2-1 formation, a system that had brought him success during his time at Parma.

Sucic and Diouf operated behind Thuram, with Barella and Çalhanoğlu forming the double pivot. However, the experiment backfired. Inter’s usual 3-5-2 offered greater central presence and allowed them to create numerical overloads, particularly when Lautaro dropped deeper to link play.

Without that additional central presence, Inter struggled to establish the same midfield superiority.

Amorim’s subtle shift from a 3-4-2-1 to a 4-4-1-1 was primarily intended to increase Milan’s presence in the wide areas.

With Inter heavily reliant on the flanks to progress their build-up, Milan used this adjustment to create numerical superiority, often establishing 4v3 situations in wide areas.

This allowed them to outnumber Inter around the ball, restrict their passing options and prevent progression. An effective example of horizontal pressing.

Much has been said about the build-up to Milan’s first goal, particularly the excellent combination play that allowed them to progress from the back and find Moreira. However, what followed was equally important.

A 2v2 situation developed in the wide areas, with Rabiot occupying Bastoni and Moreira taking on Carlos Augusto. Moreira won his individual duel, creating the opportunity to deliver into the box.

While this was unfolding, Milan committed three players into the penalty area: Ramos, Pulisic and Diawara. Pulisic’s movement was particularly intelligent. He initially checked his run, distracting Bisseck, who was more focused on the ball than tracking his opponent.

As the cross arrived, Pulisic moved into the space created by that moment of hesitation, set himself and finished clinically. A goal built on excellent individual quality and intelligent off-ball movement.

A rare set-piece goal for Milan, but one that involved the collective effort of several players. Milan used their players effectively as blockers, almost like in volleyball.

Ramos blocked Sucic, while Pavlovic and De Winter occupied Bisseck and Akanji. Diawara also engaged two Inter players, creating a completely free route between Moreira and Rabiot.

With Inter defending zonally, these blocking movements disrupted their defensive structure and left Rabiot unmarked. On cue, Rabiot attacked the space and met Moreira’s delivery to score.

A well-rehearsed set-piece routine built on intelligent movement and effective blocking.

Milan then moved to a 5-2-3 shape to defend the obvious attack from Inter who looked to recover in the game.

With Milan maintaining a high defensive line, Inter looked to exploit Thuram’s pace by playing chipped through balls into the space behind the defence.

After going 2-0 up, Milan took a significant defensive risk with their approach. The front three of Rabiot, Pulisic and Ramos continued to press high, while the back five held their position.

This created a considerable gap between the two units, which Inter were able to exploit during their counter-attacks.

Inter used rotations in the build-up to create numerical advantages in the wide areas. Barella dropped into the back three, allowing Bisseck to push forward and join Diouf and Spence on the right. This created a 3v2 against Diawara and Pavlovic, with Diawara particularly exposed to a 2v1.

The Nerazzurri replicated the same movement on the opposite flank, with Bastoni advancing and allowing Carlos Augusto to push higher up the pitch. This created the space for Augusto to deliver the cross that led to Djed Spence’s chance.

Inter scored their only goal from a corner. Calhanoglu delivered an inswinging cross, with Akanji making a decoy run towards the near post and flicking the ball on with his head. This movement attracted Milan’s defenders towards the front post, leaving Bastoni unmarked at the far post to head home.

Musah did well to position himself between the ball and Barella, winning a free kick in a dangerous area. Maignan also positioned two Milan players between Inter’s wall and Josep Martinez, obstructing the goalkeeper’s line of sight.

Moreira struck underneath the ball with the upper part of his instep, generating enough lift to send it over the wall and make it 3-1.

With Milan comfortably ahead, Amorim’s priority was to manage the game, and he did so effectively. He dropped the defensive line by around four metres and encouraged Milan to circulate possession more in their own half, avoiding unnecessary risks while Inter were forced to chase the game.

Milan also played more long balls in the second half, reflecting their increased willingness to exploit the spaces left behind by Inter through counter-attacks.

Inter were initially outnumbering Milan in central areas, but Amorim addressed the issue with a tactical adjustment. He instructed Pulisic and Rabiot to drop deeper, forming a midfield triangle that provided additional central support and prevented Inter from creating the same numerical overloads.

Amorim also introduced adjustments to neutralise the wide overloads created by Bisseck and Bastoni. He repositioned Pulisic deeper, asking him to track Bisseck’s movements and prioritise defensive duties over attacking influence. Pulisic therefore operated more like a midfielder than a traditional number 10.

Musah was given a floating role in front of the defence, acting as a screen and covering the spaces left behind whenever Milan’s defenders stepped out to engage an opponent or pushed forward to support an attack.
